However, when you're intoxicated, your vestibular system can become disrupted due to the effects of the substance. This can lead to a sensation of spinning, as your brain is trying to process information from your vestibular system in the absence of sight.

When you open your eyes, you can regain your sense of sight, and your brain can process the visual information to create a more stable sense of movement. This can help to alleviate the sensation of spinning.

It's important to note that the sensation of spinning can be quite disorienting and uncomfortable, especially if you're intoxicated a dose of the substance.

[Original Text]
The phenomenon you're describing is known as "scinopsia" or "scinopsia fugax." This is a condition where the world appears to be spinning when the eyes are closed, but when the eyes are opened, the spinning stops.

The reason behind this is that when you close your eyes, your brain is deprived of real-time visual information. As a result, it creates a mental image of the world, which is not necessarily tied to the actual environment. This mental image can be distorted, making it feel like everything is spinning.

When you open your eyes, your brain is flooded with real-time visual information, allowing it to create a clearer mental image of the world. This image is more tied to the actual environment, and the spinning sensation disappears.

It's essential to note that scinopsia is not a true medical condition, but rather a psychological phenomenon that can occur under various circumstances, including intoxication, fatigue, or stress.
